analysis.one_liner: Halts new large factory farms, forces big meatpackers to buy livestock on open markets, and restores country-of-origin meat labels.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Booker with three cosponsors in January 2020, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze new large factory farms (called concentrated animal feeding operations) and shut the largest existing ones down by 2040, offering farmers $10 billion a year in grants to pay off farm debt and switch to pasture-based or crop farming. It would rewrite the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act so meatpackers must buy at least half the animals they slaughter on the open spot market instead of through their own captive supply networks, ban packers from owning livestock outright, restrict the poultry 'tournament' pay system that pits growers against each other, and let farmers sue and recover attorney fees. It would also restore mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef and pork and extend them to dairy, and reserve the 'Product of USA' label for animals born, raised, and slaughtered here.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent ranchers and hog producers, who get more buyers bidding for their animals on open markets; contract poultry and hog growers, who get protection from one-sided contracts, the tournament pay system, and retaliation for speaking up; neighbors of large factory farms, who get the integrator companies held liable for waste and pollution instead of the farmer; and consumers, who get country-of-origin labeling on beef, pork, and dairy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent farmers, contract growers, rural neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Bars large CAFOs from starting or expanding and requires the largest existing ones to cease operating as large CAFOs by January 1, 2040, with up to $10,000 per day in civil penalties for violations [S3].

Creates a voluntary program providing $10 billion a year in grants to farm owners to pay off debts incurred to build their animal feeding operation and convert the land to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production, conditioned on a permanent easement keeping the site out of CAFO use [S3].

Requires large meatpackers to slaughter at least 50 percent of the animals at each plant through spot-market purchases from non-affiliated producers at a firm, openly bid price, phasing up from 20 percent in 2020-2021 [S3].

Makes it an unlawful practice for a packer to own or feed livestock (with narrow exceptions), to restrict growers' right to a jury trial or full damages, to terminate contracts without a real basis, or to use a poultry tournament pay formula based on factors outside the grower's control — and allows growers to sue with attorney fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs [S3].

Makes integrator companies — not contract growers — responsible and liable for dead animal disposal, manure, air and water pollution, harm to growers and third parties, and health and property-value damage to neighbors, and requires integrators to jointly hold Clean Water Act permits for farm discharges [S3].

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and bars any 'Product of USA' label unless the animal was exclusively born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies and poultry integrators, whose captive livestock supply chains and tournament pay systems would be curtailed and who would absorb pollution liability; operators and financiers of large factory farms, whose facilities could not expand and must wind down by 2040; and taxpayers, who would fund the $10 billion-a-year transition grant program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpackers, poultry integrators, large CAFO operators, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The transition program transfers $10 billion from the Treasury every October 1 with no end date and without further appropriation, a very large open-ended federal commitment [S3].

Mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork was previously repealed by Congress in 2015 after Canada and Mexico won a World Trade Organization dispute and were authorized to retaliate against U.S. goods, so restoring it risks renewed trade retaliation — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

The CAFO moratorium and 2040 phase-out would force consolidation in the opposite direction if small and mid-size operators cannot absorb the animals, and could tighten meat supply and raise consumer prices during the transition; critics also argue Americans benefit from the low prices that integrated large-scale production delivers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are real and specific: open-market price discovery for ranchers, enforceable contract rights for growers, pollution liability shifted to the companies that actually control the farms, and honest labeling for shoppers. The costs are also real — an open-ended $10 billion annual grant program, a risk of trade retaliation over labeling, and possible meat price pressure during the transition from large-scale production. The design choices (which sectors pay, who gets the grants) would determine whether the burden lands mostly on companies or partly on consumers and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on January 21, 2020 [S1][S5].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry — the only action it ever received [S5].
Three senators cosponsored it: two Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators kept their captive livestock supply chains, tournament pay systems, and limited pollution liability unchanged, and large factory farms continued to expand without restriction.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Farm System Reform Act in the Senate on January 21, 2020.

against.name: Sen. Pat Roberts
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; it received no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Meatpacking and poultry industry groups
against.role: Large beef, pork, and poultry processing companies and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's spot-market purchasing mandate, packer ownership ban, grower contract protections, and country-of-origin labeling, which they argued would raise costs and disrupt supply chains.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; no Republican supported it.

industries.industry: Meatpacking companies (beef, pork, and poultry processors)
industries.note: The bill would force packers to buy at least half of the animals they slaughter on the open spot market, ban them from owning or feeding livestock, and expose them to grower lawsuits with attorney fees — unwinding the captive supply arrangements that give the largest packers steady, cheap animals. Consumers and ranchers benefit from the price transparency that costs them.

industries.industry: Poultry and hog integrators (companies that contract with growers)
industries.note: The bill would ban tournament pay systems based on factors growers cannot control, restrict one-sided contract terms, make integrators jointly liable for farm pollution and neighbor harms, and require them to co-permit farm discharges. Their business model depends on shifting costs and risk onto contract growers.

A moratorium on starting or expanding large CAFOs and a 2040 shutdown deadline, with $10,000-a-day penalties, directly caps this sector; owners could take voluntary debt-forgiveness grants to exit, so the bill both constrains them and pays them to leave.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers and contract growers
industries.note: Open-market bidding, contract rights, jury trial protections, and liability rules shift bargaining power and pollution risk back toward the farmers who raise the animals. Their gain comes directly out of packers' and integrators' control.
$10 billion a year in transition grants would pay existing CAFO owners to convert land to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production, building these sectors' land base.
